• Common name: Vallisneria
  • Other names: Eelgrass, Tape grass, Vals or Vallis, Wild-celery
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Optimal lighting: Medium
  • Substrate: Any
  • Growth rate: Moderate to fast
  • Placement in tank: Background
  • Size: 20 to 40+ cm
  • Fertilizers: Not needed to low
  • CO2: Not needed to low
  • Propagation: By runners
  • Colour: Green

Vallisneria species are easy to find in local aquarium stores and online. Choose the variety according to the size of your tank and where you want to place it. For a small tank, go for Vallisneria nana, Vallisneria asiatica or Vallisneria spiralis, which stay relatively small. The larger Vallisneria gigantea is only recommended for larger aquariums.

The species are quite similar, and vendors may sometimes get the labels wrong. Look closely at the plants or reviews before buying, and make sure the specimens have fresh leaves and roots; avoid plants with brown foliage.

Quarantine

Unless you are completely sure the plant is safe, for example it was grown in vitro in an undamaged, unopened pot, quarantine and disinfect it first. Do not introduce a new plant to the tank right after buying it. It can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly or damselfly nymphs, etc.), and may contain pesticide residues used to remove parasites and snails, which are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates. If you disinfect Vallisneria, be careful with bleach, as it is more sensitive to it; use weaker concentrations or other methods.

Vallisneria has a cosmopolitan distribution: its diverse species are found in North America, South America, Africa, Eurasia and Australia, throughout the tropical and subtropical regions of the world. Vallisneria nana is native to Australia.
The genus contains hydrophytes, plants that live submerged in water bodies. They are found in slow to fast-moving rivers, streams, lakes and wetlands.

Even Vallisneria nana or Vallisneria natans (one of the smallest Vals) will grow large. The minimum tank size for growing Vallisneria is therefore 40 litres. A larger tank is needed for large species such as Vallisneria gigantea, otherwise it may grow enough to choke the tank.

For smaller tanks, Dwarf sagittaria looks quite similar but is much smaller.

Vallisneria is easy to care for because it adapts quickly to different conditions. It is also one of the few aquarium plants that can be grown in brackish water.

Substrate and fertilisation

It will grow in anything, including plain gravel or sand, as long as fish and snails produce enough waste; then you may not need fertiliser at all. It is not a heavy root feeder, but a nutrient-rich substrate benefits it, especially if there is not enough natural bioload and you do not want to add fertiliser. A sand substrate slows its spread, as it is harder for roots and runners to spread.

In the early stages Vallisneria appreciates fertilisers and root tabs, especially on a plain substrate. Root tabs contain macro- and micronutrients that promote strong roots, help plantlets start well and keep established plants flourishing. Place them midway into the gravel bed and replace as per the instructions. Liquid fertilisers such as Seachem Flourish and Iron provide nutrients. Be very careful with products containing glutaraldehyde (such as Seachem Flourish Excel), as this plant is quite sensitive to it. If you must choose between liquid fertiliser and root tabs, choose root tabs, since Vallisneria is a root feeder.

Planting

Place the roots under the substrate and keep the crown (where the leaves emerge) just above the substrate to prevent rot. Plant with tweezers or bare fingers, preferably in plain gravel or coarse sand: plug the plant into the substrate, then pull it out a little so only the roots stay underneath. For best results, plant in small groups in the mid-ground or background.

Trimming

Vallisneria produces vertical shoots rapidly and these shade smaller plants. Prune the tops of overgrown leaves with trimming scissors. Apart from shading, there is no need for constant pruning. Trimmed leaves heal to some degree but often do not continue to grow; instead, the plant regrows new leaves that eventually replace the damaged ones. Use sharp scissors, otherwise badly cut or ripped leaves may die back entirely.

Tip: long plants can be hard to trim, but it is easy when done together with a water change: lower the water level to use it as a measure, pull the leaves upright and trim about at water level.

Problems

  • Chlorosis: the leaves lose their normal green colour due to iron deficiency or poor lighting.
  • Rot: the crown may rot if buried too deep in the substrate, which can lead to the plant's death.
  • Melting: Vallisneria reacts badly to unstable CO2 levels and low nitrate. The plants gradually decline and the leaves wither. Melting of leaves is also common just after planting, mostly due to changes in water conditions when the tank's water chemistry differs from the previous environment. Recovery may take a while, but if the roots are in good shape the plant will take off once settled. Do not start fertilising right after planting, as this can make things worse; give it time to recover from transplant shock.
  • Red colouration in the leaves: many species may change colour under too much light or when there are not enough nutrients.

Temperature: optimal 20 – 28 °C; it is known to tolerate 15 – 30 °C.

pH: ideal 6.5 – 8.0. It does not grow well in too acidic conditions.

Hardness: it tolerates hard and soft water equally, but thrives best at 4 – 18 GH.

Light: although often recommended even for low-light planted tanks, this is not optimal. Vallisneria appreciates moderate to high lighting (30 – 50 PAR). Low light encourages the leaves to grow tall, closer to the light. Bright light helps the plants keep vibrant green leaves and boosts the growth of lateral shoots.

CO2 and fertilisation: additional CO2 injection helps keep Vallisneria healthy and positively influences growth; the leaves become thicker and more vibrant. Root tabs should be used to provide extra nutrition and curb nutrient deficiency, as this plant is a heavy root feeder. Vallisneria does not tolerate the recommended dose of liquid CO2 well: there are many reports of melting with liquid CO2, and Seachem Excel is often blamed. If you use it, increase the dose gradually and watch for a reaction.

If you keep shrimp in the tank, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilisers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Benefits and uses

  • Aquascape: a good choice for a jungle-style aquascape.
  • Foraging place: it serves as a foraging ground for fish, shrimp and snails, and a surface for biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Shelter: shrimp and small fish use it as cover and a place to lay eggs.
  • Nutrient removal: as a relatively fast-growing plant it absorbs harmful compounds from animal waste, decayed plant matter and tap water, such as nitrate, CO2, ammonia and heavy metals.
  • Oxygenation: helps oxygenate the water column.
  • Algae control: it is greedy for nutrients and outcompetes algae, reducing the chance of algal bloom.

Tankmates

Vallisneria has coarse, leathery leaves, so most plant-eating fish will not eat it. Only bottom-digging fish can damage it by pulling the roots out of the substrate, and aggressive fish can still tear it apart, so it is not recommended for a cichlid tank or a tank with aggressive fish.

It thrives in freshwater tanks with livebearers and egg scatterers, where the dense bushes serve as spawning places and shelter. Aquarium snails and dwarf shrimp also love this plant and crawl on the leaves without harming it.

  • Peaceful fish: Otocinclus catfish, pygmy corydoras, neon tetras, guppies, cherry barbs, green swordtails, rasboras, red or blue wagtail platies, etc.
  • Shrimp: practically any shrimp, including Neocaridina (Red Cherry, Blue Velvet, Black Rose, Snowball, Orange Sakura, Green Jade, Rili, etc.), Caridina (Crystal Red, Caridina cf. babaulti, Blue Tiger, etc.), Amano, ghost, bamboo and vampire shrimp.
  • Snails: ramshorn, nerite, Malaysian trumpet, Japanese trapdoor and mystery snails. Be careful with snails that can harm or try to devour the plant.

Avoid hostile, aggressive diggers that tear up plants, such as silver dollars, oscars and cichlids. Crayfish and crabs are destructive to plants and will eat and uproot everything in the tank; floating plants are the best choice for such tanks.

Vallisneria propagates vegetatively through stolons or runners. Once the plant settles, numerous runners spread all over the tank, and daughter plants develop and send off runners as well. Under optimal conditions runners can develop in only a few days. They can be clipped off the main plant for planting or disposal. Vallisneria also reproduces by flowering and seed production, although this is rarely seen in the aquarium.

Vallisneria is a genus of aquatic plants in the family Hydrocharitaceae, a flowering plant family with 16 known genera and about 135 known species that includes the tape grasses and the common or European frogbit. It was first described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753 and named in honour of Antonio Vallisneri, an Italian medical scientist, physician and naturalist.

It is a classic aquarium plant and one of the most popular and easily obtained plants in the hobby. It is used to add vertical accents in the background of planted tanks, and some varieties can be used in the mid-ground. It has a tall rosette structure, bright ribbon-like green leaves and spreads rapidly with prolific runners. It is quite undemanding and the easiest in the genus to care for.

Vallisneria are submersed perennial plants found in freshwater and brackish regions, mostly tall with ribbon or tape-like leaves growing from a basal meristem. They are dioecious: a single plant has either male or female flowers. The female flowers grow on long, thin, spirally coiled scapes, are inconspicuous, greenish and float on the water surface, whereas the male flowers develop at the base. The leaves are bright green, long, wide or narrow depending on the species, and rise to the surface where they can form dense green tangles suitable for the breeding of some fish. The tallest species produce firm ribbon-shaped leaves 30 mm wide.

Popular species

  • Vallisneria americana (gigantea), also known as Giant val or Jungle val: it has a bulb-shaped rhizome with a tangle of not very long roots. From it emerge 10 – 15 ribbon-like leaves about 20 – 35 mm wide and up to 1 m long or more, bright green, usually with 15 longitudinal obliquely connected veins. Because of its size it is only suitable for large, tall aquariums. It grows fast but propagates more slowly than other Vallisneria species and prefers slightly higher temperatures than the other common species.
  • Vallisneria nana: native to Australia. It has dark green, narrow leaves (less than 1 cm wide) and is shorter than most other Vals (25 – 40 cm). It has a distinct grass-like appearance and takes longer to get established. It is suitable as a mid-ground or background plant in small tanks.
  • Corkscrew Vallisneria (Vallisneria torta): one of the longest varieties in the hobby, growing up to 50 cm tall. It has twisted, spiral leaves and tends to be a little more compact than other species. The leaves are light green and somewhat transparent, creating a beautiful contrast when planted in groups. They are finely serrulate and substantially shorter than in some other species.
  • Vallisneria spiralis, also known as Straight Vallisneria: bright green ribbon-shaped leaves, usually with five longitudinal veins, 5 – 12 mm wide and 40 – 50 cm long, though they can grow even longer in its natural habitat. The name 'spiralis' refers to the flower stalk, not the leaves. Vallisneria spiralis var. leopard has wider, thicker leaves with stripes or spots. Under favourable conditions it propagates rapidly and fills the background with dense growth.

Sagittaria or Vallisneria?

The two are easily confused when small. Differences:

  • Sagittaria has thicker leaves, especially towards the base; Vallisneria leaves are thinner and flatter.
  • Sagittaria leaves are more opaque; Vallisneria leaves are more translucent.
  • On Sagittaria you can feel the central vein as a small ridge down the middle of the leaf; the vein of Vallisneria is barely noticeable.
  • Vallisneria leaves have small hook-like structures (almost like hairs) near the tip; Sagittaria leaves do not.
  • Vallisneria sends runners above the substrate, while Sagittaria does it under the substrate.
